current_example.title: Example: Solving an Initial Value Problem in a Defective Case

q-80912.name: Question 1
q-80912.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).$
q-80912.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

q-80912.html:
Question 1
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[−100−1]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t+c2[01]et,c1,c2∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]te−t+c2[10]e−t,c1,c2∈R
c
x(t)=c1[10]e−t+c2[01]e−t,c1,c2∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]etc1∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t,c1∈R
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e−t+c2[01]e−t,c1,c2∈R.
q-80912.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case

q-80910.name: Question 2
q-80910.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
q-80910.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

q-80910.html:
Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[230023]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e3t/2+c2[01]e3t/2,c1,c2∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e−3t/2+c2[01]e3t/2,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2t/3+c2[01]e−2t/3,c1,c2∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R.
q-80910.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case

q-80599.name: Question 3
q-80599.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t).$
q-80599.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

q-80599.html:
Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[−400−4]x(t).

a
x(t)=c1[10]e−4t+c2[01]e−4t,c1,c2∈R
b
x(t)=c1[10]e−2t+c2[01]e−2t,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]te−4t+c2[01]t2e−4t,c1,c2∈R
d
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e−2t,c1,c2∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e4t+c2[01]e−4t,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e−4t+c2[01]e−4t,c1,c2∈R.
q-80599.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case

q-80908.name: Question 4
q-80908.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
q-80908.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t/3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t/3},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

q-80908.html:
Question 4
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[−1300−13]x(t).

a
x(t)=c1[10]e−t/3+c2[01]e−t/3,c1,c2∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t/3,c1∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[01]et/3,c1∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e−3t+c2[01]e−3t,c1,c2∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t/3+c2[01]et/3,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e−t/3+c2[01]e−t/3,c1,c2∈R.
q-80908.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case

q-80548.name: Question 5
q-80548.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).$
q-80548.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

q-80548.html:
Question 5
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[2002]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2tc1∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e−2t,c1,c2∈R
c
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t,c1∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]te2t,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R.
q-80548.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case

q-80919.name: Question 6
q-80919.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
q-80919.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1+1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 4{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{4},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{4}.$

q-80919.html:
Question 6
?

Consider the system of linear differential equations given by x′(t)=[−104−1]x(t).

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

x(t)=c1[a1]e−t+c2([a1]te−t+[b0]e−t),c1,c2∈R,

what is the value of a+b?

a
14
b
−34
c
4
d
0
e
−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−104−1].

Since A is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is λ=−1 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[0040]∼[0010]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[01].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−1+104−1+1][w1w2]=[01][0040][w1w2]=[01]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {0w1+0w2=04w1+0w2=1

So, we obtain w1=14.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w=[140].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[01]e−t+c2([01]te−t+[140]e−t),c1,c2∈R.

Finally, we see that a=0,b=14, and a+b=14.

q-326237.name: Question 7
q-326237.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ b\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
q-326237.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =4$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}4-4 & 5 \\ 0 & 4-4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{w}_{2}=1 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{5},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{5}.$

q-325120.name: Question 8
q-325120.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
q-325120.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}2-2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=1,$ and $a+b=1.$

q-80604.name: Question 9
q-80604.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
q-80604.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}1+1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{w}_{1}+4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ -1{w}_{1}-2{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-2{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=-2,b=-1,$ and $a+b=-3.$

q-80604.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the system of linear differential equations given by x′(t)=[14−1−3]x(t).

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

x(t)=c1[a1]e−t+c2([a1]te−t+[b0]e−t),c1,c2∈R,

what is the value of a+b?

Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is λ=−1.

a
−1
b
2
c
1
d
0
e
−3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[14−1−3].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ=−1 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[24−1−2]∼[2400]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[−21].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[1+14−1−3+1][w1w2]=[−21][24−1−2][w1w2]=[−21]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {2w1+4w2=−2−1w1−2w2=1

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain w1=−1−2w2.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w1=−1, and therefore w=[−10].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[−21]e−t+c2([−21]te−t+[−10]e−t),c1,c2∈R.

Finally, we see that a=−2,b=−1, and a+b=−3.

q-80606.name: Question 10
q-80606.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =1.$*
q-80606.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2-1 & 9 \\ -1 & 4-1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3{w}_{1}+9{w}_{2}=3 \\ -1{w}_{1}+3{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=3{w}_{2}-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=3,b=-1,$ and $a+b=2.$

Question 10
?

Consider the system of linear differential equations given by x′(t)=[−29−14]x(t).

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

x(t)=c1[a1]et+c2([a1]tet+[b0]et),c1,c2∈R,

what is the value of a+b?

Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is λ=1.

a
2
b
1
c
−1
d
−3
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−29−14].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ=1 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[−39−13]∼[−3900]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[31].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−2−19−14−1][w1w2]=[31][−39−13][w1w2]=[31]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {−3w1+9w2=3−1w1+3w2=1

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain w1=3w2−1.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w1=−1, and therefore w=[−10].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[31]et+c2([31]tet+[−10]et),c1,c2∈R.

Finally, we see that a=3,b=−1, and a+b=2.

q-80929.name: Question 11
q-80929.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-3.$*
q-80929.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2+3 & 1 \\ -1 & -4+3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}+{w}_{2}=-1 \\ -{w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={e}^{-3t}\,[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-3t} \\ (1-t){e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-80929.html:
Question 11
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−21−1−4]x(t),x(0)=[01]. Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is λ=−3.

a
 [te−3t(1−t)e−3t]
b
 [4te−3t(1+t)e−3t]
c
 [te−3t(1−2t)e−3t]
d
 [4te−3t(1−2t)e−3t]
e
 [te−3te−3t]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−21−1−4].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ=−3 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[11−1−1]∼[1100]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[−11].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−2+31−1−4+3][w1w2]=[−11][11−1−1][w1w2]=[−11]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {w1+w2=−1−w1−w2=1

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain w1=−1−w2.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w1=−1, and therefore w=[−10].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[−11]e−3t+c2([−11]te−3t+[−10]e−3t),c1,c2∈R.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[01]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=[−c1−c2c1][01]=[−c1−c2c1][c1c2]=[1−1].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=e−3t[−11]−[−11]te−3t−[−10]e−3t=[te−3t(1−t)e−3t].

q-80617.name: Question 12
q-80617.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}5-5 & 0 \\ -1 & 5-5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ -1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{5t} \\ (2+t){e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[50−15]x(t),x(0)=[−12].

a

b
 x(t)=[(t−1)e5t2e5t]
c

d

x(t)=[−e5t(2+t)e5t]

Incorrect

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[50−15].

Since A is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is λ=5 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[00−10]∼[0010]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[01].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[5−50−15−5][w1w2]=[01][00−10][w1w2]=[01]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {0w1+0w2=0−1w1+0w2=1

So, we obtain w1=−1.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w=[−10].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[01]e5t+c2([01]te5t+[−10]e5t),c1,c2∈R.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[−12]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=[−c2c1][−12]=[−c2c1][c1c2]=[21].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=[02]e5t+[01]te5t+[−10]e5t=[−12]e5t+[01]te5t.=[−e5t(2+t)e5t].

q-80616.name: Question 13
q-80616.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2+2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}-1{w}_{2}=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ -{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ -{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1+t){e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-80616.html:
Question 13
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−2−10−2]x(t),x(0)=[1−1].

a
 [(1+2t)e−2t(2t−1)e−2t]
b
 [(1+t2)e−2t(2t−1)e−2t]
c
[(1+t)e−2t−e−2t]
d
 [(1+t)e−2t−(1+2t)e−2t]
e
 [e−2t−e−2t]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−2−10−2].

Since A is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is λ=−2 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[0−100]∼[0100]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[10].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−2+2−10−2+2][w1w2]=[10][0−100][w1w2]=[10]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {0w1−1w2=10w1+0w2=0

So, we obtain w2=−1.

The variable w1 is a free variable. Setting w1=0, we get w=[0−1].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e−2t+c2([10]te−2t+[0−1]e−2t),c1,c2∈R.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[1−1]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=[c1−c2][1−1]=[c1−c2][c1c2]=[11].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=[1−1]e−2t+[11]te−2t=[(1+t)e−2t−e−2t].

q-80928.name: Question 14
q-80928.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
q-80928.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-7+1 & -4 \\ 9 & 5+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{w}_{1}-4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ 9{w}_{1}+6{w}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+5([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 15\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1-10t){e}^{-t} \\ (1+15t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−7−495]x(t),x(0)=[11]. Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is λ=−1.

a
[(1−10t)e−t(1+15t)e−t]
b
[(1−2t)e−te−t]
c
[e−t(1+15t)e−t]
d
[e−te−t]
e
[(1−2t)e−t(1+3t)e−t]

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−7−495].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ=−1 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[−6−496]∼[3200]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[−23].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−7+1−495+1][w1w2]=[−23][−6−496][w1w2]=[−23]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {−6w1−4w2=−29w1+6w2=3

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain w1=13−23w2.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w1=13, and therefore w=[130].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[−23]e−t+c2([−23]te−t+[130]e−t),c1,c2∈R.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[11]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=[−2c1+c233c1][11]=[−2c1+c233c1][c1c2]=[135].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=13[−23]e−t+5([−23]te−t+[130]e−t)=[11]e−t+[−1015]te−t=[(1−10t)e−t(1+15t)e−t].

q-326239.name: Question 15
q-326239.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}5-5 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 4{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{4} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{4} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}]\,t{e}^{5t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\,{e}^{5t} \\ (2-12t)\,{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[5045]x(t),x(0)=[−32].

a
[−3e5t(2+12t)e5t]
b
[−3e5t(2−12t)e5t]
c
[(−3−12t)e5t2e5t]
d
[−3e5t(2−6t)e5t]
e
[−3e5t2e5t]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[5045].

Since A is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is λ=5 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[0040]∼[0010]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[01].

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue λ and only one linearly independent eigenvector v, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by x(t)=c1veλt+c2(vteλt+weλt), where w is a solution to the equation (A−λI)w=v.

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[5−5045−5][w1w2]=[01][0040][w1w2]=[01]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {0w1+0w2=04w1+0w2=1

So, we obtain w1=14.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w=[140].

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[01]e5t+c2([01]te5t+[140]e5t),c1,c2∈R.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[−32]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=[c24c1][−32]=[c24c1][c1c2]=[2−12].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=[02]e5t+[0−12]te5t+[−30]e5t=[−32]e5t+[0−12]te5t=[−3e5t(2−12t)e5t].
